title: Don't let our hearts swerve
hook: our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You guided us (3:8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, muhkam: the clear, firm verses, the mother of the Book, and others left open. Your line was some verses are for sitting with. Did you leave one thing open instead of deciding? Day three hundred sixty-four, the end of a week.

Yesterday's verse carried a warning: some people have a swerve in their hearts, and chase what's unclear. And the very next verse doesn't point a finger at them. It turns around and asks for help. Commentators hear the people who were just praised, those firmly rooted in knowledge, as the ones speaking. Their first worry isn't other people's hearts. It's their own. If anyone feels safe from drifting, it should be them. They don't.
screen: `A SWERVE IN THE HEART.` → `THE NEXT VERSE TURNS AROUND.` → `NOT THEIR HEARTS. OURS.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, 3:8 begins: "Our Lord! Cause not our hearts to stray after Thou hast guided us." Then it asks for mercy from God's own presence, and ends: You are the Bestower. Notice the link. Yesterday's verse said zaygh, a swerve, in the hearts of some. Today's asks la tuzigh, don't let them swerve. It's the same root, z-y-gh: to lean, to tilt away from straight. One verse describes the tilt; the next asks to be kept from it. Notice, too, the timing in the request: after You guided us. It isn't a prayer for people who are lost. It's for people who've already found the way and know that finding it once isn't the same as staying on it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported, in a hadith in Tirmidhi, to have often said: O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon your religion. Anas, who reports it, says the companions asked whether he feared for them, and he said yes: hearts are held between two of God's fingers, and He turns them as He wills. In the hadith's Arabic, Turner of hearts is muqallib al-qulub, and both words share one root, q-l-b, to turn over: the heart is named as the thing that turns. So the request is honest about how hearts work. Some Muslims say 3:8 in their own supplications after the prayer. And it closes a week that has been about keeping things: a man raised after a hundred years, a grain that multiplies, charity not spoiled by reminders, a debt written down, a burden that fits, verses held firm or held open. Today, a heart kept straight.
screen: `THE SWERVE, AND THE REQUEST` · `Z-Y-GH: TO TILT AWAY` · `AFTER YOU GUIDED US` · `QALB: THE THING THAT TURNS` · then, large: `OUR LORD! CAUSE NOT OUR HEARTS TO STRAY.`

segments.voice: If you pray, you can say 3:8 after your next prayer, in Arabic or in your own language: rabbana la tuzigh qulubana. For now, when the bell starts, sit up straight, and feel how small the movements are that keep you upright: a lean forward, a correction back. Nobody sits perfectly still. Think of one place this week where your heart tilted a little, toward impatience, envy, or carelessness. Don't scold it. Just notice the lean, and come back to center. The bell holds the time.
Don't let our hearts swerve. The request of 3:8, made by people already guided, asking to stay that way. Today's word.
screen: `DON'T LET OUR HEARTS SWERVE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep my heart straight. Today, when you notice yourself leaning, toward a sharp word or an old habit, take that as the moment to correct, not to give up. Day three hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Many Muslims say the supplication of 3:8, 'rabbana la tuzigh qulubana', after the daily prayers and in personal du'a, along with the Prophet's reported prayer to the Turner of hearts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer to be shown the way.
what it means: a prayer by people already guided, asking not to drift from it.
what a scholar hears: la tuzigh answers the zaygh of 3:7, the same root; and qalb, heart, from a root about turning, echoed in the hadith of the Turner of hearts.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the Tirmidhi 2140 scene was misreported (the companions asked whether he feared for them, not why he said it so often; the wording there is 'fingers of Allah', not 'of the Most Merciful', which is Muslim 2654), now fixed; the qalb etymology is now anchored in the hadith's own phrase muqallib al-qulub instead of 'Muslim teachers have long made the point'; 'many Muslims' became 'some'; the speakers of 3:8 are now attributed to the commentators; 3:7 'ended on a warning' corrected to 'carried a warning' (it ends on 'men of understanding').
